new_statements.quote: The two main prosodic features in Agarabi are tone and nasalisation. Stress is predictable. There are two degrees of tone, high and low. These are primarily level tones though a slight glide on a phonetically short vowel may be perceived when there is a transition from one level to another in succeeding syllables. Otherwise, pitch glides occur only on phonetically long vowels and are interpreted as a sequence of low-high or high-low tones.
new_statements.citation: Goddard, Jean. 1980. Notes on Agarabi grammar. In M. Boxwell, J. Goddard, M. Ross, A. Sanders, J. Sanders & H. Davies (eds), Papers in New Guinea Linguistics No. 20, 35-76. Pacific Linguistics A-56. Canberra: Research School of Pacific and Asian Studies, Australian National University. DOI 10.15144/PL-A56.35.
new_statements.locator: p. 39, section 1.2 'Prosodic features' (PDF page 5 of the ANU bitstream)
new_statements.reading: tone language with a stress statement
new_statements.rule_in_words: Agarabi is described as a two-tone (high/low) language in which stress is non-contrastive ('predictable'). The source does not say where the predictable stress falls; no placement rule, no examples with stress marks, and no relation to tone is stated. Tone (acute = high) is the marked prosody in citation forms.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned for stress. For tone: pitch glides on short vowels are treated as transitions between levels; glides on long vowels as LH or HL sequences; fn. 8 notes tone perturbation across word boundaries is marked only inside phonetic brackets.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description of prosodic features in a grammar sketch; examples are isolated words in phonetic brackets with tone marked by acute. Nasalisation is the other prosody and is discussed at length; stress gets the single sentence.
new_statements.identity_note: Goddard's data are from Punano village, Kainantu Sub-District, Eastern Highlands (Goddard 1967 introduction, fieldwork 1960-65); the SIL 2002 OPD calls the language 'Bare (Agarabi)' and the ANU recordings spell it 'Agarabe'. All refer to the same language-level languoid agar1252 (ISO agd); no dialect is singled out.
